Ca(II)-Catalyzed Cascade Reaction of Tryptamines with Propargylic
Alcohols: Temperature-Driven Ring Opening and Closing via the
Allene Migration Pathway for the Synthesis of Pyrrolo[1,2‑a]indoles
Ashok Kale, Su Jeong Kwon, Joohan Lee, Jae Kyun Lee, and Kyeong Lee*
Cite This: Org. Lett. 2024, 26, 1196−1200

ABSTRACT: A temperature-dependent cascade of reactions between tryptamines and propargylic alcohols was developed to
achieve selective formation of pyrroloindoline and pyrrolo[1,2-a]indole heterocycles by Ca(II) catalysis. The cascade consists of
electrophilic addition of allene at the C3 carbon of indole followed by intramolecular cyclization at 60 °C to yield pyrroloindolines.
Furthermore, simultaneous 1,2-allene migration and pyrrolidine ring opening were followed by intramolecular cyclization via C−N
bond formation at reflux temperature to obtain pyrrolo[1,2-a]indole scaffolds. A wide range of substrates, a clean reaction profile,
scalability, and good to excellent yields are the advantages of this protocol.
I

importance in synthetic chemistry owing to their broad
biological profile and versatile chemical reactivities.
1
Among
them, the pyrroloindoline core structure is found in numerous
natural products (Figure 1)
2
and is a common structural motif
among secondary metabolites of terrestrial and marine origin.
3
Especially, C3 carbon-derived pyrroloindoline shows a
distinctive range of chemical and biological properties. For
example, Calycanthaceae plant extracts have been used as
traditional Chinese medicines for the treatment of fungal
infection,
4

matory conditions.
5

and their scaffolds are an important class of privileged
structural units that are found in many natural products and

14

except for NHTs, the tryptamines remaining failed to produce
the desired product; this fact might be due to the stability of
the partial pyramidalization of the sulfonamidate in the

16
Propargylic alcohols prepared from aliphatic
ketones and acetophenone could not produce the correspond-
ing products due to less reactivity under standard reaction
conditions (low temperature).
After assessing the generality of the reaction with various
tryptamines and propargylic alcohols (Table 2), an experiment
was conducted at reflux temperature for the exclusive
formation of the intermediate C followed by intramolecular
cyclization to obtain the possible products 4a or 5a.
Interestingly, the formation of pyrrolo[1,2-a]indole (com-
pound 5a) was observed (Scheme 3) which was confirmed by
NMR, HRMS, and single-crystal X-ray data (5d) (Figure 2).
With this result, we attempted to optimize the reaction
conditions to obtain the desired compound 4a using
intermediate C, but no results were satisfactory. Experiments
were subsequently conducted to optimize 5a with a
stoichiometric ratio of catalyst, additive, and other catalysts
such as Sc(OTf)

yield, but no change in the yield of 5a was observed (Table 3,
entries 10−13). Using the optimized reaction conditions for
the synthesis of 5a, the substrate scope was evaluated by
reacting to various substituted tryptamines NHTs, NHCOCF
3

3
, and NHBoc (Table 4). However, in the reaction
using NHBoc tryptamine, Boc deprotected product 5z was
observed under standard conditions due to the Ca(II) reagent
and high temperature. Furthermore, propargylic alcohols
prepared from aliphatic alkynes failed to give the desired
products. This might be due to the lack of migration efficiency
of allene. These results showed that this protocol produced the
desired compounds in high yields (Table 4). After the
successful formation of 5a, a gram-scale reaction was further
performed to assess the practicality of this protocol during the
scale-up process (Scheme 4). Therefore, we performed the
reaction with 3.1 mmol of 1a (1 g) and 2a under standard
reaction conditions (Table 3, entry 2) and isolated 1.75 g of
5a. Furthermore, a stepwise mechanistic study was conducted
for the formation of 5a. Initially, a model reaction was carried
out at 90 °C for 12 h to isolate intermediate C. However, a
mixture of products was obtained (3a 25%, C 56%, and 5a
10%). Then the same reaction was repeated, and after 12 h, the
reaction mass was further heated to reflux temperature.
Surprisingly, exclusive formation of 5a was observed with a
yield of 93%. These results showed that compound 3a was also
converted to 5a at the reflux temperature, and this was
reconfirmed by the reaction of 3a under standard conditions
(Scheme 5).
The synthetic utility of the selected compounds of 5 is
demonstrated by treating 5d with phenylboronic acid under
Suzuki cross-coupling conditions to give compound 7. In
addition, conducting an acid−amine coupling reaction of 5z
with 3-chlorobenzoic acid leads to the formation of 9 (Scheme
5).
The detailed reaction mechanism for the formation of 3 and
5 is shown in Scheme 6. Initially, Ca(OTf)
2
/Bu
4
NPF
6
activated propargylic alcohol 2 undergoes an S
N
2
1
reaction
with 1 that results in iminium A. Intramolecular cyclization of
A leads to the formation of 3a via C−N bond formation of
NHTs with imine carbon. Next, 1,2-allene migration followed
by pyrrolidine ring opening leads to B, which on β-H
elimination forms 2-allenyltryptamine C. Finally, intermediate
C undergoes cyclization via a 5-exo-dig manner to produce 5.
In conclusion, we demonstrated selective product formation
at different temperatures by Ca(II)-catalyzed cascade reactions
of tryptamines and propargylic alcohols via pyrrolidine ring
opening by C−C bond, allene migration, and a new C−N
bond formation mechanism. In addition, we evaluated the role
of Bu
4
NPF
6
and detailed mechanistic studies were conducted
to support the formation of pyrrolo[1,2-a]indoles. Further-
more, the proposed protocol was scalable, and mild reaction
conditions, low reaction time, easy procedures, a wide range of
substrate scope, and high yields are the advantages of this
protocol.
